```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5
)
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(unimlsurv)
  library(mlr3)
})
```

`unimlsurv` is the time-to-event counterpart to `uniml`. It keeps the same
layering — specification, data, task, learners, tuning, metrics, plots, workflow
— so if you know one package you know the other. What changes is the outcome and
therefore what "correct" means.

This vignette uses a simulated cohort with a known truth throughout, so every
number can be checked against the model that generated it.

## What a survival outcome is

Two columns, not one:

* the follow-up **time**: how long a patient was observed;
* the **status**: `1` if the event happened at that time, `0` if the patient was
  censored at that time.

Censoring is why survival statistics are not classification statistics. A patient
censored at 10 months is not a patient who survived 10 months and it is not a
patient who died at 10 months. Every metric in this package either drops
censored patients from a comparison it cannot inform (the concordance index) or
weights them by the inverse of the censoring survival (Brier score, time-dependent
AUC, calibration, decision curves).

```{r data}
data <- sim_surv_data(n = 400, seed = 2026)
head(data, 4)
```

The simulator stores the true linear predictor, so we can also ask what the best
possible answer looks like:

```{r truth}
time_points <- c(12, 36, 60)
truth <- sim_surv_truth(data, time_points)
round(head(truth$survival, 3), 3)
```

## The specification comes first

`surv_spec()` builds a `uniml_spec` with `task_type = "survival"` and adds a
`survival` block. Preprocessing, tuning, and learners are configured with the
same functions as in `uniml`, because they are the same functions.

```{r spec}
spec <- surv_spec(
  time = "time",
  status = "status",
  time_points = time_points
)
spec <- uniml::set_preprocess(spec, impute = "median_mode", scale = "zscore")
spec <- surv_set_learners(spec, c("coxph", "rpart"), tune = FALSE)
spec
```

The time points are yours to choose and are never invented by the package. They
should be the horizons a clinician would ask about, not round numbers chosen for
convenience.

## Data and task

```{r task}
prepared <- as_surv_data(data, spec)
prepared

task <- make_surv_task(prepared, spec)
task
```

`as_surv_data()` drops rows with a missing time or status rather than imputing
them: an imputed outcome is not an outcome. Feature values may still be missing,
and those are imputed during preprocessing, on the training data only.

## The metrics, one at a time

```{r metrics}
learner <- mlr3::lrn("surv.coxph")
fitted <- train_surv(task, learner)
prediction <- fitted$predict(task)

survival <- survival_matrix(prediction, time_points)
risk <- survival_risk(prediction)

metrics <- calc_surv_metrics(
  prepared$time, prepared$status, risk, survival, time_points
)
metrics$overall
metrics$by_time
```

Read the table like this:

* `cindex` is Harrell's concordance index: pick two patients where one had the
  event first; the C-index is the probability the model gave the sicker one the
  higher risk. 0.5 is a coin flip.
* `brier` at a time point is the inverse-probability-of-censoring weighted mean
  squared difference between the predicted survival probability and what
  happened.
* `auc` at a time point is the cumulative/dynamic AUC: the probability that a
  patient who had an event by that time was given a higher risk than a patient
  who was still event-free after it.
* `ibs` integrates the Brier score over the time points you asked for.

Every one of these is pinned by a test against an independent implementation:
`survival::concordance()` for the C-index, `riskRegression::Score()` for the
Brier score and the AUC. The AUC is additionally pinned against the area under
the ROC curve the package itself draws, so the number and the figure cannot
disagree.

## Calibration

Discrimination asks "who is sicker"; calibration asks "is the number right". A
model can rank perfectly and still tell every patient they have a 90% chance of
surviving.

```{r calibration}
calibration <- surv_calibration_curves(
  prepared$time, prepared$status, survival, time_points
)
calibration$summary
head(calibration$table, 4)
```

`ici` is the integrated calibration index: the patient-weighted mean absolute
difference between the prediction and the Kaplan-Meier estimate inside each
prediction group. Groups are formed from the predictions only, never from the
outcome.

The summary also carries `slope` and `intercept`, which answer a sharper
question than the group table and do not depend on how the groups were cut:

```{r calibration-slope}
surv_calibration_slope(prepared$time, prepared$status, survival[, 1], time_points[1])
```

`surv_calibration_slope()` fits
`cloglog(P(T <= t | x)) = intercept + slope * cloglog(1 - S(t | x))`. The
complementary log-log link is the scale on which a proportional hazards model is
additive, so a calibrated prediction gives a slope of 1 and an intercept of 0.
Below 1 means the predictions are too extreme, above 1 means too timid, and a
non-zero intercept means the whole curve sits too high or too low. Patients
censored before the horizon carry no information about the binary outcome at that
horizon and are dropped, and the rest are weighted by the inverse Kaplan-Meier
censoring survival — the same weighting as the Brier score.

Read the `n` and `events` it returns before reading the coefficients. This
cohort has enough patients to estimate them, but a slope from a few dozen
patients can sit far from 1 while the model is fine, because the spread of the
predicted survival on the cloglog scale is small and the fit mostly amplifies
noise. Roughly 100 patients with a few dozen events is the point at which the
number starts to mean something; below that, report the reliability curve and
skip the coefficient.

```{r calibration-plot, fig.cap = "Time-point calibration against Kaplan-Meier survival, with the recalibration coefficients in the caption."}
plot_surv_calibration(calibration)
```

## Decision curves

A model is only useful if acting on it beats acting on everybody and beats
acting on nobody.

```{r dca}
dca <- surv_dca_curves(prepared$time, prepared$status, survival, time_points)
plot_surv_dca(dca)
```

Net benefit is computed with the same inverse-probability-of-censoring weights,
so a patient censored before the horizon is not counted as a certain non-event.

## Discrimination over time

```{r time-metrics, fig.cap = "Brier score and time-dependent AUC over time."}
plot_surv_km(data, spec, group = "sex")
```

The Kaplan-Meier curves show the crude picture. What the model adds is the
separation the covariates buy.

## The workflow

`run_surv_workflow()` runs the shared `uniml` engine — the same code that
prepares, tunes, and predicts for the binary workflow — and then scores the
results with the survival metrics. The validation set selects, the test and
external sets report.

```{r workflow}
set.seed(42)
index <- sample.int(nrow(data))
train <- data[index[1:280], ]
validation <- data[index[281:340], ]
test <- data[index[341:400], ]

result <- run_surv_workflow(spec, train = train, validation = validation,
                            test = test)

result$metrics[, c("model", "set", "cindex", "ibs", "brier_36")]
result$ranking
```

`rpart` reports a C-index and nothing else. That is not a bug: `surv.rpart` can
only produce a risk score, so it cannot be asked for a Brier score. The package
says so in `result$meta$notes` instead of quietly filling in a number.

```{r notes}
result$meta$notes
```

## Confidence intervals

Every number in the table above is a point estimate. The workflow bootstraps the
comparison set for you; `surv_ci()` does the same thing on any prediction you
already have.

```{r ci}
head(result$ci[, c("model", "metric", "mean", "lower", "upper", "n_effective")], 6)
```

Patients are resampled, not rows of a metric table. A resample that loses the
cases or the controls a time point needs returns `NA` and is counted in
`n_effective`, so a narrow interval can never come from a handful of lucky
resamples.

## Explaining the model

A survival model does not predict one number, so a SHAP analysis has to say what
it is explaining. `time_point = NULL` explains the risk score — the quantity the
concordance index ranks, and the one the published survival SHAP examples
explain. A time point explains the predicted survival probability at that horizon
instead.

```{r shap-risk}
explained <- surv_shap(
  result, validation, model = "coxph",
  n_explain = 60, bg_n = 30, seed = 1
)
explained
plot_surv_shap_beeswarm(explained)
```

```{r shap-time, fig.cap = "SHAP dependence for the predicted 36-unit survival."}
explained_36 <- surv_shap(
  result, validation, model = "coxph", time_point = 36,
  n_explain = 60, bg_n = 30, seed = 1
)
plot_surv_shap_dependence(explained_36, "x1")
```

The two explanations are not interchangeable: a feature can raise the risk score
and lower S(36) by different relative amounts, and the ranking of features can
differ between them. Report which quantity you explained.

```{r shap-importance, fig.cap = "SHAP importance for the risk score."}
plot_surv_shap_importance(explained)
```

`plot_surv_shap_waterfall()` and `plot_surv_shap_force()` explain one patient at
a time, which is what a case discussion needs.

## Handing the model to someone else

Subgroup analyses are not part of this package on purpose: which subgroups matter
is a clinical decision, and a package that guesses is worse than one that does not.
What the package does is hand over everything needed to do it properly.

```{r save, eval = FALSE}
path <- uniml::save_result(result, "model.rds")
```

The file holds the fitted learners, the fitted preprocessor, the selected
features, and the specification. Whoever opens it can score any subset and use the
same metric functions the workflow used:

```{r subgroup, eval = FALSE}
restored <- uniml::read_result("model.rds")
older <- validation[validation$age > 50, ]
scored <- predict_surv(restored, older)
calc_surv_metrics(
  older$time, older$status, scored$risk,
  as.matrix(scored[, grep("^S_", names(scored))]),
  restored$meta$time_points
)
```

## Which learners are available

`surv_learner_registry()` lists every `surv.*` learner the installed `mlr3`
packages expose, with a short alias, whether it can produce survival
probabilities, and whether it has a curated tuning search space.

```{r registry}
available <- surv_learner_registry(available_only = TRUE)
available[, c("key", "mlr3_key", "distr", "tunable")]
```

```{r registry-count}
nrow(surv_learner_registry())
```

A learner without a curated space is still usable, just fitted at its defaults;
`surv_register_learner()` adds a search space when you want to tune it.

Predicting new patients uses the fitted preprocessor and the fitted learner, and
never refits anything on the new data:

```{r predict}
newdata <- data[index[341:350], ]
predict_surv(result, newdata, model = "coxph")
```

`model = "best"` would pick whatever ranks first, and here that is `rpart`, which
cannot produce survival probabilities. The error names the models that can, which
is more useful than silently switching to a different model than you asked for:

```{r predict-best, error = TRUE}
predict_surv(result, newdata)
```

## Exporting a result

The result is a `uniml_result`, so the export layout is the one you already know:

```{r export, eval = FALSE}
uniml::export_results(result, dir = tempfile("unimlsurv-"))
```

## What is deliberately missing

* **Competing risks.** A patient who dies of something else is not censored;
  they had an event, of a different type. That changes the estimate, not just the
  implementation, so it is out of scope here.
* **Uno's IPCW C-index.** It is a different estimand from Harrell's C and the
  two should not be confused; only Harrell's C is reported.
* **Subgroup analyses.** Which subgroups matter is a clinical decision, not a
  statistical default. The package gives you a saved model and a scorer instead of
  inventing the groups.
* **Tuning on the Brier score.** The inverse-probability weights depend on the
  censoring distribution of the data the model was fitted on, so tuning models on
  it would compare numbers computed on different data. Tuning uses the
  concordance index.

See `system.file("REFERENCES.md", package = "unimlsurv")` for the full list of
papers each statistic follows.
